records.title: Solver Parameter Input File
records.text: Solver Parameter Input File The svMultiPhysics solver reads simulation parameters from a text file in Extensible Markup Language (XML) format. The XML file structurally organizes the svMultiPhysics solver parameters and input data (e.g. mesh files) needed to set up and execute a simulation. What is XML The XML format is made up of tags, elements and attributes. A tag begins with . There are two types of tag start-tag, such as &ltsection> end-tag , such as &lt/section> An XML element is everything from (including) the element's start tag to (including) the element's end tag. <Tolerance> 0.001 </Tolerance> There are three types of elements text attributes - name-value pair within a start-tag: name="value" " other elements - elements nested within other elements The following XML is an example of these different element types <Add_mesh name="fluid"> <Mesh_file_path> fluid_mesh.vtu </Mesh_file_path> <Add_face name="inlet"> <Face_file_path> inlet.vtp </Face_file_path> </Add_face> <Domain> 1 </Domain> <Mesh_scale_factor> 0.1 </Mesh_scale_facto> </Add_mesh> The above contains six elements: Add_mesh, Mesh_file_path, Add_face, Face_file_path, Domain and Mesh_scale_factor <Add_mesh name="fluid"> has an attribute name with value "fluid" <Add_mesh name="fluid"> element provides a context for the other elements under it: <Add_face name=inlet&gt associates the face named inlet to the mesh named fluid Mesh_file_path is a text element with text fluid_mesh.vtu Domain is a text element with text 1 Mesh_scale_factor is a text element with text 0.1 How svMultiPhysics uses XML For the svMultiPhysics solver input file the XML elements are used as the names of the solver parameters. svMultiPhysics defines for each parameter Name - Case sensitive with the first letter capitalized Data type boolean - on, off integer - numeric with no decimal string - a contiguous list of characters real - numeric with decimal or scientific notation Context - parameters can only be found within the context of another parameter If a value for a parameter is not valid svMultiPhysics will display an error message indicating where in the file the error occurred. Some parameters are optional. There are two types of optional parameters Used if not set - a default value is used Not used if not set - no default value The organization of the parameter input file The parameter input file is organized into six sections used to provide context for the parameters defined under them <GeneralSimulationParameters> - General Simulation Parameters <Add_mesh> - Mesh Parameters <Add_equation> - Equation Section <LS> - Linear Solver Parameters <Output> - Output Parameters The parameter input XML file must start with the following two lines <?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8" ?> <svMultiPhysicsFile version="0.1"> and end with the single line </svMultiPhysicsFile> where <?xml - identifies the file as an XML format file <svMultiPhysicsFile - identifies the file as an svMultiPhysics XML format file The following outlines the basic structure of the parameter input XML file. < GeneralSimulationParameters > [general parameters] < /GeneralSimulationParameters > < Add_mesh name= mesh_name_1 > < Add_face name= mesh1_face_name_1 > < Add_face name= mesh1_face_name_2 > &nbsp... < Add_face name= mesh1_face_name_n > < /Add_mesh > < Add_mesh name= mesh_name_2 > < Add_face name= mesh2_face_name_1 > < Add_face name= mesh2_face_name_2 > &nbsp... < Add_face name= mesh2_face_name_n > < /Add_mesh > ... < Add_mesh name= mesh_name_N > < Add_face name= meshN_face_name_1 > < Add_face name= meshN_face_name_2 > &nbsp... < Add_face name= meshN_face_name_M > < /Add_mesh > < Add_equation type= eq_1 > [equation parameters] < Domain id=0 > < Domain id=1 > ... < Domain id=N > < LS type= ls_type > &nbsp[linear solver parameters] < /LS > < Output type= output_type > &nbsp[solver output parameters] < /Output > < /Add_equation > Parameter Documentation Conventions Parameters are documented using the parameter Name and DataType . If the parameter is optional its default value is shown between square brackets Example The optional Spectral_radius_of_infinite_time_step parameter with default value 0.5 <Spectral_radius_of_infinite_time_step> real [0.5] </Spectral_radius_of_infinite_time_step> A string parameter will have a default value of none . If not set the parameter will have a value of an empty string ("" in C++) and will be treated as being unset and will not be used. Example The optional Save_results_in_folder string parameter with default value none <Save_results_in_folder> string [none] </Save_results_in_folder> A required parameter will have no default value. Example The required Number_of_time_steps parameter with no default value <Number_of_time_steps> integer </Number_of_time_steps> Solver Parameter Input File Examples The svMultiPhysics GitHub repository Test Cases directory contains solver input XML files used to test svMultiPhysics. These XML files can be used as templates that can be customized for a particular application.

records.title: svZeroDSolver Interface Subsection
records.text: svZeroDSolver Interface Subsection The svZeroDSolver Interface Subsection of the Equation Section defines the parameters needed by the svMultiPhysics solver to interface with the svZeroDSolver. The SimVascular svZeroDSolver simulates bulk cardiovascular flow rates and pressures using an arbitrary zero-dimensional (0D) lumped parameter model (LPM) of a discrete network of components analogous to electrical circuits. It provides an Application Programming Interface (API) that allows it to communicate and interact with external software applications directly using function calls to programmatically define custom inflow and outflow boundary conditions for a CFD simulation. The svMultiPhysics solver can directly access the svZeroDSolver API by loading the svZeroDSolver as a shared (dynamic) library available after installing the svZeroDSolver. In order to couple svMultiPhysics with the svZeroDSolver, you will need to provide a json file containing the LPN to couple the 3D domain to. Documentation on how to structure this json file can be found in the svZeroDSolver documentation See the pipe_RCR_sv0D svMultiPhysics test case for an example of using the svZeroDSolver interface for an RCR boundary condition in a simple fluid simulation. The svZeroDSolver Interface Subsection is organized as follows < svZeroDSolver_interface > [ svZeroDSolver Interface Parameters ] < /svZeroDSolver_interface > The svZeroDSolver_interface keyword activates coupling for boundary conditions with the < Time_dependence > Coupled < /Time_dependence > keyword for the enclosing equation coupled boundary condition. svZeroDSolver Interface Parameters <Coupling_type> string [none] </Coupling_type> The type of coupling used between the svMultiPhysics and svZeroDSolve solvers. The coupling type determines how contributions from the coupled svZeroDSolver are added to the svMultiPhysics solver tangent matrix. The value of the coupling type can be explicit - No contribution is added. This may potentially cause poor nonlinear convergence. implicit - Contributions are added as outlet resistances for each svZeroDSolver and svMultiPhysics solver Newton iteration. This leads to theoretically quadratic nonlinear convergence but at the expense of additional computation. semi-implicit - Contributions obtained from the svZeroDSolver for outlet resistances are added only at the beginning of the simulation . <Configuration_file> string [none] </Configuration_file> The name of the svZeroDSolver JSON configuration file containing the description of the components of a lumped parameter network and various simulation parameters. <Shared_library> string [none] </Shared_library> The path and name of the svZeroDSolver shared library used to access the svZeroDSolver API. The name of the library is specific to the computer platform you are using Linux - libsvzero_interface.so MacOS - libsvzero_interface.dylib Windows - libsvzero_interface.dll On MacOS and Linux this library will be installed in the directory /usr/local/sv/svZeroDSolver/DATE/lib. <Initial_flows> real [0.0] </Initial_flows> Initialize the flows for all coupling blocks with the given value. If this parameter is not given then flows will not be initialized. <Initial_pressures> real [0.0] </Initial_pressures> Initialize the pressures for all coupling blocks with the given value. If this parameter is not given then pressures will not be initialized.

records.title: Domains Panel
records.text: Domains Panel The Domains panel is used to assign a finite element mesh to a physical domain used in the simulation. Files are assumed to be stored in a mesh-complete directory containing the finite element volume and boundary faces mesh files. Panel Layout Usage Add Mesh-Complete Button - Selecting this button brings up a file browser used to select the mesh-complete directory containing finite element mesh files. The volume mesh and boundary surface faces stored there will be added to the simulation. The boundary surface faces will be displayed in the Face List: ListTable . Domain ComboBox - Select the current domain. Multiple domains may be read in by selecting more than on mesh-complete directories (e.g. fluid-solid simulation). Type: Ratio Button - Selects the domain physics as a fluid or solid . Face List: ListTable - Lists the boundary surface face names defined for a domain. These are the names of the files in the mesh-complete/mesh-surfaces directory and will later be used to identify the faces used for boundary conditions.

records.title: SimVascular MultiPhysics Tool
records.text: SimVascular MultiPhysics Tool The SimVascular SV MultiPhysics Tool is used to interactively create the mesh and solver XML input files needed to run an svMultiPhysics simulation. The MultiPhysics Tool stores data in the Project /svMultiPhysics/ Data Node directory. The MultiPhysics Tool stores values input via the GUI controls into the Project MultiPhysics/ Data Node .multiphysicsjob file. The following sections describe how to use the SimVascular MultiPhysics Tool GUI to set the mesh, boundary conditions, material properties and solver parameters needed for a simulation. See the Getting Started / Introduction documentation for a description of the SimVascular graphical user interface (GUI) controls and useful application Tools concepts. Creating Mesh Files The MultiPhysics Tool requires files containing the finite element volume mesh (VTK VTU) and boundary surface meshes (VTK VTP). These files are created by by right-clicking on the Meshes node under the SV Data Manager. Selecting the Export Mesh Complete menu item displays a file browser used to select to location to store the location for the finite element files. Creating a MultiPhysics Tool Instance Creating a MultiPhysics Tool is performed differently than the other Tools. First select the MultiPhysics Icon locationed in the SimVascular Window Toolbar. This will bring up an uninitialized MultiPhysics Tool panel Next select the button at the top of the MultiPhysics Tool panel. This will display a Create MultiPhysics Job popup window. The Create MultiPhysics Job popup menu. Type fluid_simulation into the Job Name DialogBox . This names is used to identify the MultiPhysics Tool instance and to name the files and directories stored under the SimVascular project's MultiPhysics directory. Selecting OK creates an MultiPhysics Tool instance node under the SV Data Manager. Selecting this instance displays the MultiPhysics Tool panel. The MultiPhysics Tool panel. The panel contains four buttons at the top used to primarily to create new svMultiPhysics simulations (jobs) New job Button - Selecting to create a new MultiPhysics instance Save job Button - Select to write the values of GUI controls into the SVPROJECT /MultiPhysics Job Name .multiphysicsjob file. Load job Button - Select to display a file browser used to select a .multiphysicsjob file. The values of GUI controls are then set from the values in this file. Load mesh - Reads in the finite element mesh stored in the Project /Meshes directory. At startup SimVascular does not read in the finite element mesh so this must be initiated manually. The panel contains four sub-panels used to input a specific category of data needed to create the files needed to run a svMultiPhysics solver simulation Domains Physics Simulation Parameters Run Simulation A selecting a sub-panel name brings up the sub-panel's controls. The following sections describe how each of the sub-panels are used.

The following sections describe how to use the SimVascular MultiPhysics Tool GUI to set the mesh, boundary conditions, material properties and solver parameters needed for a simulation. records.title: SimVascular MultiPhysics Tool Tutorial
records.text: SimVascular MultiPhysics Tool Tutorial This tutorial will demonstrate how to set up and run a simulation for the fluid flow in a cylinder. The steps required to do this are Create finite element mesh files Create an instance of a MultiPhysics Tool Add the finite element mesh files used to define a domain representing a 3D fluid region Add a fluids equation used to solve 3D flow Add quantities to output during the simulation The SimVascular Cylinder Project Example will be used for the model and mesh data referenced in the following discussion. SimVascular does not automatically save data created by a Tool to the Project . If a Project is closed without being saved all newly added data will be lost. Open the CylinderProject SimVascular Description Start the SimVascular application, read in the CylinderProject project and set the graphics view to a single 3D view. Select the Data Manager Models cylinder Data Node to bring up the SV Modeling panel. The Face List GUI control panel shows that the cylinder model has three faces (boundary surfaces) named wall - cylinder wall surface outlet - cylinder outlet surface inlet - cylinder inlet surface Creating Mesh Files The finite element mesh has already been created for this example project. The MultiPhysics Tool requires files containing the finite element volume mesh (VTK VTU) and separate (VTK VTP) files containing the boundary surface meshes. The following steps demonstrate how to create a directory containing these finite element mesh files. SimVascular Description SimVascular does not automatically load finite element mesh data so we will use the GUI to manually load it. Right-click on the Meshes/cylinder Data Node under the SV Data Manager and select the Load/Unload Volume Mesh menu item. The mesh is displayed in the 3D graphics window. Right-click on the Meshes/cylinder Data Node under the SV Data Manager and select the Export Mesh Complete menu item. A file browser is displayed and used to select to location to store the finite element files. This creates a cylinder-mesh-complete directory containing the finite element mesh files cylinder-mesh-complete ├── mesh-complete.exterior.vtp ├── mesh-complete.mesh.vtu ├── mesh-surfaces │ ├── inflow.vtp │ ├── outlet.vtp │ └── wall.vtp └── walls_combined.vtp where mesh-complete.mesh.vtu - volume mesh mesh-surfaces/inflow.vtp - boundary mesh for the inflow model face mesh-surfaces/outflow.vtp - boundary mesh for the outflow model face mesh-surfaces/wall.vtp - boundary mesh for the wall model face These files will be used to define the finite element mesh for the MultiPhysics simulation. Creating an MultiPhysics Tool Instance The SimVascular MultiPhysics Tool comprises the GUI controls used to create the files needed to run a simulation. The following steps demonstrate how to create an instance of an MultiPhysics Tool . SimVascular Description Select the MultiPhysics Icon located on the SimVascular window Toolbar . This displays an MultiPhysics Tool panel. From the MultiPhysics Tool panel select the New Job Button . A popup DialogBox is displayed. Type fluid_simulation into the job Name DialogBox . Select the OK Button . A new MultiPhysics Tool instance Data Node named fluid_simulation is created under the SV Data Manager . The fluid_simulation name is used to identify the MultiPhysics Tool instance and to name the files and directories stored under the SimVascular CylinderProject's MultiPhysics directory. Double-clicking on the MultiPhysics Tool fluid_simulation Data Node brings up its MultiPhysics panel containing its GUI controls. The panel contains four sub-panels used to input a specific category of data needed to create the files needed to run a svMultiPhysics solver simulation Domains Physics Simulation Parameters Run Simulation Selecting a sub-panel name brings up the sub-panel's controls. The following sections demonstrate how to use each of these sub-panels. Adding a Domain The Domains panel is used to assign a finite element mesh to a physical domain used in the simulation. SimVascular Description Select the Add Mesh-Complete Button . A file browser is displayed used to select to location of the finite element files directory. Select the directory created above and then select the Open Button . The boundary surfaces (faces) inflow , outlet and wall are displayed in the Face List: Table . These names are taken from the names of the VTK VTP files store in the cylinder-mesh-complete/mesh-surfaces directory. Adding a Fluids Equation The following steps demonstrate how use the Physics panel to set the equation to solve, set physical properties and change output quantities. SimVascular Description Select the Physics Tab . This brings up the Physics Sub-panel. Select the Incomp. fluid item from the Add or remove equations left List . Next select the Button to add an incompressible fluids equation to the simulation. The Incomp. fluid item has been moved from the Add or remove equations left List to the right List and the equation has been added to the simulation. The Properties , Outpu t BCs , Advanced , Linear Solver and Remesher Buttons at the bottom of the Add or remove equations lists set applicable to the currently selected equation in the right List . Selecting the Properties Button brings up a Physical properties panel that is used to set the values if the fluid's physical properties used in the simulation. Selecting the Output Button brings up a Add or remove outputs panel that is used to set the quantities output during the simulation. Velocity and Pressure quantities are output by default and are therefore shown in the right List . Select the WSS item in the left List and then select the Button . The WSS item has been moved from the left List to the right List . This quantity will now be output during the simulation. Adding Boundary Conditions The following steps demonstrate how set boundary conditions for the fluids simulation. The inlet boundary condition is a constant flow rate of 100 cc/sec into the face named inflow . The flow will have a parabolic spatial profile across the inflow face. SimVascular Description Selecting the BCs Button brings up a Boundary conditions panel that is used to add boundary conditions to the simulation. Selecting the Add Button at the bottom of the Boundary conditions panel brings up the Boundary Conditions Setup popup that is used to add a boundary condition. The Face list List in the popup shows the faces read in as boundary surfaces from the cylinder-mesh-complete directory. Selecting a face name enables setting the parameters and data used to define a boundary condition. The following actions are then performed to set the appropriate parameters for a constant parabolic flow into the inflow face: Select the inflow face name from Face list List . Select Dirichlet from the BC Type ComboBox . Check the Steady CheckBox . Type 100 into the Value TextBox . Select the Parabolic CheckBox . Select the OK Button at the bottom of the popup. The inflow face boundary condition now appears in the Boundary conditions panel. Now select the Add Button at the bottom of the Boundary conditions panel. The following actions are then performed to set the appropriate parameters for a resistance boundary condition for the outflow face: Select the outflow face name from Face list List . Select Neumann from the BC Type ComboBox . Check the Resistance CheckBox . Type 1330.0 into the Value TextBox . Select the OK Button at the bottom of the popup. The outflow face boundary condition now appears in the Boundary conditions panel. Setting Simulation Parameters The following steps demonstrate how set the simulation parameters for the fluids simulation. For this tutorial we will run the fluids simulation for 500 time steps, saving results to VTK-format files every 10 time steps. SimVascular Description Select the Simulation Parameters Tab . This brings up the Simulation Parameters Sub-panel. The following actions are then performed to set the appropriate simulation parameters Type 500 into the Number of time steps TextBox . Check the Save as VTK CheckBox . Run Simulation The following steps demonstrate how to run the fluids simulation. To run the fluids simulation you must first write the solver XML file. You will then select the number of processors (cores) used to run the simulation. SimVascular Description Select the Run Simulation Tab . This brings up the Run Simulation Sub-panel.

records.text: Fluid mechanics

records.title: Strong form
Standard (Galerkin) weak form
records.text: Standard (Galerkin) weak form For the finite element method, we will first derive the Galerkin weak form for the Navier-Stokes-Brinkman equations. We define our trial and weighting function spaces, \[ u_{i} \in \tau_{i} : \\{u_{i} \in H^{1}\left(\Omega\right) \mid u_{i} = g_{i} \text{ on } \Gamma_{g_{i}}\\}, \] \[ w_{i} \in \nu_{i} : \\{w_{i} \in H^{1}\left(\Omega\right) \mid w_{i} = 0 \text{ on } \Gamma_{g_{i}}\\}, \] \[ p, q \in Q : \\{p \in L^{2}\left(\Omega\right)\\}, \] where \(\boldsymbol{w}\) is the weighting function for velocity and \(q\) is the weighting function for pressure. We represent these weighting functions discretely on a per-element-basis as \[ w_{i} = \sum_{a=1}^{n_{en}} N_{a}^{w}w_{ai}, \] \[ q = \sum_{a=1}^{n_{en}} N_{a}^{q}q_{a}, \] where \(N_{a}^{w}\) and \(N_{a}^{q}\) are the nodal shape (basis) functions for the velocity and pressure spaces, respectively, and \(w_{ai}\) and \(q_{a}\) are the associated arbitrary nodal coefficients. Similarly, the trial functions are represented by \[ u_{i} = \sum_{a=1}^{n_{en}} N_{a}^{w}u_{ai}, \] \[ p = \sum_{a=1}^{n_{en}} N_{a}^{q}p_{a}. \] We then multiply the Navier-Stokes-Brinkman equations by \(\boldsymbol{w}\) and \(q\) , respectively, and integrate by parts to obtain the standard Galerkin momentum and continuity weak forms [7] [5] , \[ \int_{\Omega} \rho w_{i}\frac{du_{i}}{dt} d\Omega + \int_{\Omega} \rho w_{i}u_{k}u_{i, k} d\Omega + \int_{\Omega} w_{i, j}\sigma_{ij} d\Omega + \int_{\Omega} \frac{\mu}{K}w_{i}u_{i} d\Omega - \int_{\Omega} w_{i}\rho b_{i} d\Omega - \int_{\Gamma_{h}} w_{i}h_{i} d\Gamma = 0, \] \[ \int_{\Omega} qu_{i,i} d\Omega = 0. \] These two equations can be added together to obtain \[ \int_{\Omega} qu_{i,i} d\Omega + \int_{\Omega} \rho w_{i}\frac{du_{i}}{dt} d\Omega + \int_{\Omega} \rho w_{i}u_{k}u_{i, k} d\Omega + \int_{\Omega} w_{i, j}\sigma_{ij} d\Omega + \int_{\Omega} \frac{\mu}{K}w_{i}u_{i} d\Omega - \int_{\Omega} w_{i}\rho b_{i} d\Omega - \int_{\Gamma_{h}} w_{i}h_{i} d\Gamma = 0. \]

records.title: Assigning Boundary Conditions
records.text: Assigning Boundary Conditions Boundary conditions specify how the fluid interacts with its bounding surfaces (faces) and are used to prescribe known values to drive fluid flow. Recall from the <Add_mesh> section that we labeled each of the exterior surfaces according to the .vtp surface mesh files. We can now use these labels to define an inflow and two outflow resistance boundary conditions as Face name Boundary condition Value cap_aorta Steady 100 mL/s cap_aorta_2 Resistance 2600 dyne . s / cm 5 cap_right_iliac Resistance 2600 dyne . s / cm 5 Boundary conditions are specified using the <Add_BC> parameter: <Add_equation type="fluid"> ... <Add_BC name="cap_aorta"> <Type>Dirichlet</Type> <Time_dependence>Steady</Time_dependence> <Value>-100</Value> <Profile>Parabolic</Profile> <Zero_out_perimeter>true</Zero_out_perimeter> <Impose_flux>true</Impose_flux> </Add_BC> <Add_BC name="cap_aorta_2"> <Type>Neumann</Type> <Time_dependence>Resistance</Time_dependence> <Value>2600</Value> </Add_BC> <Add_BC name="cap_right_iliac"> <Type>Neumann</Type> <Time_dependence>Resistance</Time_dependence> <Value>2600</Value> </Add_BC> <Add_BC name="wall_aorta"> <Type>Dirichlet</Type> <Time_dependence>Steady</Time_dependence> <Value>0</Value> </Add_BC> <Add_BC name="wall_right_iliac"> <Type>Dirichlet</Type> <Time_dependence>Steady</Time_dependence> <Value>0</Value> </Add_BC> Each <Add_BC> section specifies a condition for one of the named surfaces. The inlet face is cap_aorta , where a flow rate of $100\ \mathrm{mL/s}$ is prescribed for this example. Boundary-condition values should be chosen to match the available physiologic data and the region being modeled. Boundary conditions that specify velocity or flow are classified as Dirichlet <Type> boundary conditions. The flow rate at the inlet is not changing with time, so we specify its <Time_dependence> to Steady . The <Value> for this boundary condition is set to $-100$. We use a negative sign for the value here to specify that the flow is going into the domain. A positive flow value would have the flow exiting the domain. The <Profile> setting specifies the spatial profile for the velocity on the face. We set this to Parabolic for this case to model the Hagen-Poiseuille solution for flow of a viscous fluid in a pipe. The Hagen-Poiseuille solution has the highest fluid velocity in the center of the vessel and decreases smoothly to a value of zero at the walls. To enforce the no-slip boundary condition at the walls, we set the <Zero_out_perimeter> setting to true . Finally, to specify that this boundary condition is for the flow (and not velocity), we set the <Impose_flux> setting to true . Resistance outlet boundary conditions represent the effect of downstream vascular resistance through $P=QR$. In this example, both outlet resistances are $2600\ \mathrm{dyn\cdot s/cm^5}$. $$ P = QR $$ Pressure boundary conditions are considered Neumann <Type> . We specify a resistance outlet boundary condition by assigning Resistance in the <Time_dependence> field in the boundary condition. Equal outlet resistances are a simplifying assumption, not a guarantee of equal computed flows, because pressure losses within the three-dimensional vessels also affect the distribution. If an outlet carries approximately $50\ \mathrm{mL/s}$, the resistance relation gives approximately $100\ \mathrm{mmHg}$. The outlet flows should be checked when interpreting this calculation. $$ P=(50 \ mL/s)*(2600 \ \mathrm{dyn\cdot s/cm^5})=130000 \ dyne/cm^2 \approx 100 \ mmHg $$ $100 \ mmHg$ of pressure is roughly the average blood pressure in a healthy individual. When more specific physiologic data are available for the patient, the boundary condition values should be chosen to match those data. The last boundary conditions we need to specify are the wall conditions. This simple simulation assumes the walls are rigid which means they are fixed in space. For these cases, we apply the no slip boundary condition which states that any fluid in direct contact with the wall will have zero velocity. For both wall surfaces, we assign Dirichlet <Type> boundary conditions with a value of $0 \ cm/s$. We wish to apply this to the velocity directly, thus the <Impose_flux> setting, which was present for the inlet face, is missing here.

records.title: Adding the equation to solve
records.text: Adding the equation to solve The <Add_equation> section of solver.xml specifies the governing equation and its physical properties, boundary conditions, output settings, and numerical solution parameters. Setting type="fluid" selects the incompressible Navier-Stokes equations. The <Add_equation> section used for a steady simulation is: <Add_equation type="fluid"> <Coupled>true</Coupled> <Min_iterations>1</Min_iterations> <Max_iterations>10</Max_iterations> <Tolerance>1e-4</Tolerance> <Backflow_stabilization_coefficient>0.3</Backflow_stabilization_coefficient> <Density>1</Density> <Viscosity model="Constant"> <Value>0.04</Value> </Viscosity> For this simulation, the <Add_equation> section specifies a fluid density of $1\ \mathrm{g/cm^3}$, a Constant viscosity of $0.04\ \mathrm{Poise}$, and a backflow stabilization coefficient of $0.3$ to help control flow reversal at outlet boundaries. This Newtonian, constant-viscosity approximation is appropriate for the large arteries modeled here, although blood can exhibit non-Newtonian behavior. The mesh coordinates and dimensional input values use a consistent centimeter-gram-second (CGS) system of units in this example. <Min_iterations> and <Max_iterations> bound the nonlinear iterations within each time step, while <Tolerance> specifies a relative residual stopping criterion. A smaller tolerance can require more work, but does not by itself guarantee a more accurate physical solution. Reaching the maximum iteration count does not establish that the tolerance was satisfied. For more information about residuals and convergence, see Simulation Results Output .

records.title: Output Control and File Management
records.text: Output Control and File Management The <GeneralSimulationParameters> section contains several parameters that control how frequently restart files (for resuming simulations) and VTK results files (for visualization) are written. See Simulation Results Output for details. <GeneralSimulationParameters> ... <Restart_file_name>results</Restart_file_name> <Increment_in_saving_restart_files>10</Increment_in_saving_restart_files> <Start_saving_after_time_step>1</Start_saving_after_time_step> <Continue_previous_simulation>false</Continue_previous_simulation> <Save_averaged_results>true</Save_averaged_results> <Save_results_to_VTK_format>true</Save_results_to_VTK_format> <Name_prefix_of_saved_VTK_files>results</Name_prefix_of_saved_VTK_files> <Increment_in_saving_VTK_files>10</Increment_in_saving_VTK_files> <Spectral_radius_of_infinite_time_step>0.2</Spectral_radius_of_infinite_time_step> <Searched_file_name_to_trigger_stop>STOP_SIM</Searched_file_name_to_trigger_stop> <Simulation_requires_remeshing>false</Simulation_requires_remeshing> <Verbose>true</Verbose> <Warning>true</Warning> <Debug>false</Debug> </GeneralSimulationParameters> The most useful and important settings are: <Increment_in_saving_restart_files> - This specifies the number of time steps between saved restart files. Usually, restart files should not be saved too often, because they can take up too much space and overwhelm a file system. However, saving them periodically allows a simulation to be resumed from a recent state. <Start_saving_after_time_step> - This specifies the earliest time step eligible for saving VTK results. Files are written at eligible steps that also satisfy the VTK output interval. This setting does not delay restart files or every text-output history. <Save_averaged_results> - This flag will tell svMultiPhysics to save one file that contains time-averaged results. This can be convenient if you wish to perform time averaging across all timesteps in an unsteady simulation. <Save_results_to_VTK_format> - This flag instructs svMultiPhysics to save simulation results in VTK format for visualization in ParaView. <Increment_in_saving_VTK_files> - This specifies the number of time steps between saved VTK results files. For this steady-flow example, the results at the final time steps are of primary interest. Examining several of these results can help determine whether transient effects have subsided. For an unsteady simulation, results should be saved at sufficiently frequent intervals to capture changes over time. The other settings in this section can be adjusted for more niche cases, but these are the most useful to know for a general svMultiPhysics simulation.

records.title: Linear Solver Parameters
records.text: Linear Solver Parameters Part of the process of numerically solving the equations of fluid mechanics involves forming a very large system of linear algebraic equations. For large three-dimensional CFD problems, direct solvers can require prohibitive amounts of memory and computation, so this example uses an iterative linear solver to obtain an approximate solution. The type and settings for the linear solver can have dramatic impacts on the performance and accuracy of the simulation. More detailed information about the different linear solvers and their settings included in svMultiPhysics can be found in the linear-solver reference . For this simple example, we cover just the basics to get an idea of what each setting does. Linear solver settings are specified in a subsection in the <Add_equation> section: <Add_equation type="fluid"> ... <LS type="NS"> <Linear_algebra type="fsils"> <Preconditioner>fsils</Preconditioner> </Linear_algebra> <Max_iterations> 10 </Max_iterations> <Tolerance> 0.4 </Tolerance> <Krylov_space_dimension> 50 </Krylov_space_dimension> <NS_GM_max_iterations> 200 </NS_GM_max_iterations> <NS_GM_tolerance> 0.01 </NS_GM_tolerance> <NS_CG_max_iterations> 500 </NS_CG_max_iterations> <NS_CG_tolerance> 0.02 </NS_CG_tolerance> </LS> This simulation utilizes the NS linear solver which was developed for the specialized boundary conditions used for blood flow simulations. First, we consider all the tolerance parameters, which specify the acceptable amount of error at each stage of the linear solver. The approximate solutions to the linear system can only be solved up to a tolerance. Decreasing the tolerance generally improves the accuracy of the computed linear-system solution but may increase computation time. Separate tolerances are specified for the specialized NS linear solver as a whole, its GMRES component, and its conjugate-gradient component. In this example, these tolerances are set to 0.4, 0.01, and 0.02, respectively. The maximum number of iterations specifies how many times the linear solver may iterate to find a solution. Linear solver algorithms require several iterations to reach their solution. Additional iterations can improve the accuracy of the linear-system solution, but beyond a certain point, the improvement may not justify the computational cost. A convergence tolerance allows the solver to stop when the residual is sufficiently small, avoiding unnecessary iterations. Increasing the maximum number of iterations does not necessarily increase computational cost, because the solver stops once the tolerance criterion is satisfied.

records.title: Finite Element Mesh Files
records.text: Finite Element Mesh Files The finite element mesh used for the simulation comprises: a volume mesh of tetrahedral elements defining the three-dimensional computational domain, stored in a VTK VTU file surface meshes of triangular elements defining the two-dimensional boundary surfaces, stored in VTK VTP files The following directory structure shows the mesh files referenced by this example's solver.xml input file: demomesh-mesh-complete/ ├── mesh-complete.mesh.vtu └── mesh-surfaces/ ├── cap_aorta.vtp ├── cap_aorta_2.vtp ├── cap_right_iliac.vtp ├── wall_aorta.vtp └── wall_right_iliac.vtp The <Add_mesh> section in solver.xml associates a mesh name with its volume-mesh file and identifies the boundary surfaces and their surface-mesh files. <Add_mesh name="demomesh-mesh-complete"> <Mesh_file_path>demomesh-mesh-complete/mesh-complete.mesh.vtu</Mesh_file_path> <Add_face name="cap_aorta"> <Face_file_path>demomesh-mesh-complete/mesh-surfaces/cap_aorta.vtp</Face_file_path> </Add_face> <Add_face name="cap_aorta_2"> <Face_file_path>demomesh-mesh-complete/mesh-surfaces/cap_aorta_2.vtp</Face_file_path> </Add_face> <Add_face name="cap_right_iliac"> <Face_file_path>demomesh-mesh-complete/mesh-surfaces/cap_right_iliac.vtp</Face_file_path> </Add_face> <Add_face name="wall_aorta"> <Face_file_path>demomesh-mesh-complete/mesh-surfaces/wall_aorta.vtp</Face_file_path> </Add_face> <Add_face name="wall_right_iliac"> <Face_file_path>demomesh-mesh-complete/mesh-surfaces/wall_right_iliac.vtp</Face_file_path> </Add_face> </Add_mesh> The <Mesh_file_path> parameter sets the path to the volume mesh file used to define the 3D computational domain. A series of <Add_face> parameters are then used to assign names to the 2D boundary surfaces used for boundary conditions. The <Face_file_path> parameter specifies the path to each surface mesh file. The svMultiPhysics XML file defines parameter values; no action is performed as individual parameters are read. The entire XML file is read before svMultiPhysics attempts to load the mesh files.

records.title: Finite Element Mesh Files
records.text: Finite Element Mesh Files The finite element mesh used for the simulation comprises: a volume mesh of tetrahedral elements defining the three-dimensional computational domain, stored in a VTK VTU file surface meshes of triangular elements defining the two-dimensional boundary surfaces, stored in VTK VTP files The following directory structure shows the mesh files referenced by this example's solver.xml input file: demomesh-mesh-complete/ ├── mesh-complete.mesh.vtu └── mesh-surfaces/ ├── cap_aorta.vtp ├── cap_aorta_2.vtp ├── cap_right_iliac.vtp ├── wall_aorta.vtp └── wall_right_iliac.vtp The <Add_mesh> section in solver.xml associates a mesh name with its volume-mesh file and identifies the boundary surfaces and their surface-mesh files. <Add_mesh name="demomesh-mesh-complete"> <Mesh_file_path>demomesh-mesh-complete/mesh-complete.mesh.vtu</Mesh_file_path> <Add_face name="cap_aorta"> <Face_file_path>demomesh-mesh-complete/mesh-surfaces/cap_aorta.vtp</Face_file_path> </Add_face> <Add_face name="cap_aorta_2"> <Face_file_path>demomesh-mesh-complete/mesh-surfaces/cap_aorta_2.vtp</Face_file_path> </Add_face> <Add_face name="cap_right_iliac"> <Face_file_path>demomesh-mesh-complete/mesh-surfaces/cap_right_iliac.vtp</Face_file_path> </Add_face> <Add_face name="wall_aorta"> <Face_file_path>demomesh-mesh-complete/mesh-surfaces/wall_aorta.vtp</Face_file_path> </Add_face> <Add_face name="wall_right_iliac"> <Face_file_path>demomesh-mesh-complete/mesh-surfaces/wall_right_iliac.vtp</Face_file_path> </Add_face> </Add_mesh> The <Mesh_file_path> parameter sets the path to the volume mesh file used to define the 3D computational domain. A series of <Add_face> parameters are then used to assign names to the 2D boundary surfaces used for boundary conditions. The <Face_file_path> parameter specifies the path to each surface mesh file. The svMultiPhysics XML file defines parameter values; no action is performed as individual parameters are read. The entire XML file is read before svMultiPhysics attempts to load the mesh files.

records.title: Specifying Output Quantities
records.text: Specifying Output Quantities The <Output> parameter specifies which quantities to output to VTK files used for visualizing simulation results. Different output quantities can be selected based on the information needed from the simulation. By default, the velocity and pressure fields are output since they are the primary outputs from a fluids simulation. Wall shear stress (WSS) is another common simulation output due to its association with vascular remodeling and cardiovascular disease. The outputs are specified within a subsection of the <Add_equation> section: <Add_equation type="fluid"> ... <Output type="Spatial"> <Velocity>true</Velocity> <Pressure>true</Pressure> <WSS>true</WSS> </Output>

records.title: Running svMultiPhysics from the Command Line in a Terminal
records.text: Running svMultiPhysics from the Command Line in a Terminal A simulation can be run from the command line by executing the svMultiPhysics application binary in a terminal. For installations of svMultiPhysics on macOS or Ubuntu, the svmultiphysics application binary should be found in the following location: /usr/local/sv/svMultiPhysics/DATE/bin/svmultiphysics where DATE is the build date (e.g., 2026-06-11). Different installed versions have different build dates in their executable paths. The following command lists the installation folders: ls /usr/local/sv/svMultiPhysics/ This should show the svMultiPhysics installation folders. If multiple versions are installed, their folders should be identified by build date. The date in the executable path should match the appropriate build date. After identifying the executable, navigate to the folder containing the XML input file and run: [svmultiphysics_executable] [name_of_xml_input_file] For example, to run demo_simulation.xml using the 2026-06-11 version of svMultiPhysics , use: /usr/local/sv/svMultiPhysics/2026-06-11/bin/svmultiphysics demo_simulation.xml To run the simulation on N cores using Open MPI, use mpiexec : mpiexec -n N /usr/local/sv/svMultiPhysics/2026-06-11/bin/svmultiphysics demo_simulation.xml

records.title: Checking Simulation during Runtime
records.text: Checking Simulation during Runtime After launching a simulation, the terminal window displays information about its progress. If the simulation is diverging or taking too long, it can be stopped to investigate the problem instead of waiting until it reaches the end: Sample terminal output when running svMultiPhysics. The terminal output provides information about the simulation as it progresses. Three particularly useful parts of the output are explained below. NS xx-xx - The first two letters in this column identify the system of equations being solved. Since this simulation models only fluid flow, the solver reports NS for the Navier-Stokes equations. The next two numbers indicate the current time step and nonlinear iteration within that time step. In the screenshot, the solver advances to the next time step after four nonlinear iterations, rather than continuing to the maximum of ten iterations. The simulation ends after completing the number of time steps specified in <GeneralSimulationParameters> . The next number immediately to the right of this column shows the amount of wall-clock time that has elapsed since the simulation was launched, in seconds. The 30th time step in the simulation above started 1,892 seconds after the simulation was launched. The second number inside the square brackets [ ] represents a normalized residual relative to the first nonlinear iteration of the time step. The residual measures how closely the current numerical solution satisfies the discretized governing equations. This ratio starts at 1.0 for each time step and generally decreases as the solver converges, although it may fluctuate. The solver can advance to the next time step either when its convergence criteria are satisfied or when the maximum number of nonlinear iterations is reached. The first number in the square brackets shows the change in the residual in decibels (dB). For more details, see the svMultiPhysics documentation , under “Simulation History histor.dat File.” Monitoring the simulation residual helps assess whether the simulation is converging adequately. If the residual decreases too slowly within a time step or consistently increases, reducing the time-step size may help the simulation converge. If the time-step size is reduced, the number of time steps should also be adjusted to preserve the total simulated time. For example, halving the time-step size requires doubling the number of time steps. To stop a simulation from the command line terminal, press Ctrl+C .

records.title: Visualizing Simulation Results
records.text: Visualizing Simulation Results When a simulation finishes, the results can be viewed by loading the .vtu result files into ParaView, an open-source application for visualizing 3D data. More information about downloading and running ParaView can be found on its website . To view the results from this example, open ParaView and click “Open”. Navigate to the simulation results N-procs folder and open the file results_100.vtu . This file contains the results from the final time step. As discussed earlier, examining several of the final time steps can help determine whether transient effects have subsided. After opening the file, click the green “Apply” button on the left-hand side of the screen to load the results. The geometry should now be visible in the 3D viewing window: Paraview interface after loading .vtu results. To view a specific result field, select it from the dropdown menu near the top of the ParaView window. By default, no field is selected, and the model is displayed as Solid Color . The menu allows fields such as velocity and pressure to be displayed. While simulation results depend on the geometry and boundary conditions, there are certain expected solution characteristics that should be present in most simulations. It is usually a good idea to check these characteristics to assess whether the simulation ran as intended. First, examine the velocity field to check whether the velocity boundary conditions were applied correctly: Velocity field results on the walls from svMultiPhysics simulation with rigid walls. The vessel walls appear blue, indicating zero velocity according to the color legend. This is expected because the simulation assumes rigid, stationary walls with a no-slip boundary condition. In a deformable-wall simulation, wall motion can produce nonzero velocities at the wall. When the model is rotated to show the outlet caps, nonzero velocities should be visible there, consistent with blood flowing through the outlets. Velocity field results on the outlet caps from svMultiPhysics simulation. Next, it is useful to check the pressure distribution in the model. In general, pressure is expected to be highest at the inlets and lowest at the outlets. The decrease in pressure from the inlets to the outlets reflects energy losses due to viscous friction in the three-dimensional flow domain: Pressure field results from an svMultiPhysics simulation. There may be other factors that produce local increases or decreases in pressure, such as sudden changes in vessel radius or deformable walls. However, for this rigid-wall example, pressure should generally decrease from the inlets to the outlets. If this overall trend is absent, possible causes should be investigated before proceeding with further analysis.

records.title: Time Step Parameters
records.text: Time Step Parameters The transient (unsteady) Navier-Stokes equations are solved to describe how the velocity and pressure of the fluid evolve over time. Each time step advances the numerical solution to a new point in simulated time. The time-step size specifies the interval of simulated time between consecutive solutions. The <GeneralSimulationParameters> section of the XML file contains parameters to set the time-step size and the number of time steps for a simulation: <GeneralSimulationParameters> <Number_of_time_steps> 100 </Number_of_time_steps> <Time_step_size> 1e-3 </Time_step_size> It is important to select a <Time_step_size> value that will produce a stable and accurate solution. Similar to the mesh size, simulation accuracy goes up as the time-step size decreases (at additional computational time and cost). We choose a time-step size of $1 \ ms$ ($0.001 \ seconds$) for this example, which is a good starting point for cardiovascular simulations. Another good rule of thumb for selecting the time-step size is to use the CFL condition: $$ CFL = v * \Delta t / \Delta x < 1 $$ Here, $v$ is a characteristic velocity in the simulation, $\Delta x$ is the grid spacing for the mesh, and $\Delta t$ is the time-step size. A CFL number below 1 can be a conservative starting estimate, but it is not a universal stability requirement for the implicit time integration used by svMultiPhysics. The time-step size should also be assessed from convergence behavior and, when needed, a sensitivity check of the quantities of interest. An unstable solution will diverge , meaning the errors will grow exponentially until the simulation eventually crashes. The stability of a simulation can be monitored in real time by observing the residual , which will be explained in a future section. The CFL number is normally hard to compute exactly for a given simulation since the grid spacing is not uniform and the velocity changes at different locations in a simulation. If a simulation is diverging, reducing the time-step size and re-running the simulation may help. The number of time steps, together with the time-step size, determines the total simulation time. For this simple simulation, we are simulating $100$ time steps at $0.001$ seconds each, so the total simulation time is $(100 \ timesteps)(0.001 \ s/timestep) = 0.1 \ s$. Several final time steps should be inspected for remaining changes in pressure and flow before treating the result as steady. By contrast, if the boundary conditions are changing with time, as in a simulation with pulsatile inflow, it is necessary to simulate a larger number of time steps to run multiple cardiac cycles. The next example will demonstrate how to simulate multiple cardiac cycles with pulsatile inflow boundary conditions.

records.title: Other Parameter Changes for Unsteady Simulation
records.text: Other Parameter Changes for Unsteady Simulation The simulation duration and output settings are specified in the <GeneralSimulationParameters> section. <Number_of_time_steps> and <Time_step_size> determine how much simulated time is covered. A fresh simulation starts from its specified initial conditions, which need not represent the established pulsatile solution. Initial-condition effects must diminish before the repeating response is analyzed; these effects are distinct from the physiological changes that should remain within each cardiac cycle. This example runs for four cardiac cycles, with the final cycle intended for analysis. Four cycles are a starting choice, not a guarantee that initial-condition effects have subsided. Compare pressure or flow at corresponding phases of successive cycles to check whether appreciable cycle-to-cycle changes remain. A longer run may be needed. If earlier-cycle VTK results are not retained, this comparison requires suitable saved boundary histories or a run that retains additional cycles. The example cap_aorta.flow file spans one second, corresponding to 60 cycles per minute. With a time-step size of $1 \ ms$, $4000$ time steps simulate four full cardiac cycles: … <Number_of_time_steps>4000</Number_of_time_steps> <Time_step_size>1e-3</Time_step_size> … The output interval must provide enough temporal resolution for analysis without producing unnecessarily many files. As in Example 1, restart files and VTK results have separate saving intervals: … <Increment_in_saving_restart_files>10</Increment_in_saving_restart_files> <Start_saving_after_time_step>3000</Start_saving_after_time_step> … <Save_averaged_results>true</Save_averaged_results> <Save_results_to_VTK_format>true</Save_results_to_VTK_format> <Name_prefix_of_saved_VTK_files>results</Name_prefix_of_saved_VTK_files> <Increment_in_saving_VTK_files>10</Increment_in_saving_VTK_files> … The restart and VTK saving intervals remain 10 time steps, as in Example 1. <Start_saving_after_time_step> is changed to $3000$ to limit VTK output to the final simulated cycle; it does not delay restart files. With a time-step size of 0.001 seconds, VTK snapshots are spaced 0.01 seconds apart. A one-second cycle spans 100 snapshot intervals; the number of saved files depends on whether both endpoints are included. Saving averaged results remains enabled, which can be convenient for analysis.

records.title: RCR Outlet Boundary Conditions
records.text: RCR Outlet Boundary Conditions An RCR boundary condition combines a capacitance with proximal and distal resistances to provide a lumped approximation of the downstream vascular impedance. Capacitance models how vessels can temporarily store and release blood as their volume changes with pressure. This lumped model does not reproduce wave propagation along deformable vessel walls. RCR outlet boundary conditions are also called three-element Windkessel boundary conditions: RCR Windkessel outlet boundary condition. RCR boundary conditions require values for three parameters: proximal resistance $(R_p)$, capacitance $(C)$, and distal resistance $(R_d)$. This example allocates initial outlet resistance estimates inversely to outlet area, with 10% assigned to proximal resistance and 90% to distal resistance. The derivation and worked values are provided in the optional RCR resistance-allocation appendix . The actual flow split also depends on pressure losses in the three-dimensional domain and the outlet boundary conditions. The other component of the RCR model is the capacitor. With a pure resistance condition, the pressure drop is proportional to the flow through that outlet. With capacitance, the relationship between pressure and flow also depends on storage, which can change waveform shape, including amplitude and timing. This figure illustrates how a lumped compliance element can alter the relationship between pressure and flow: Illustration of changes in pressure and flow waveform amplitude and timing with a lumped compliance element. The capacitance is a parameter of the lumped outlet model that needs to be selected. Available pressure measurements can guide its adjustment, but it cannot generally be determined from a mean pressure and flow alone. Unlike the mean resistance estimate, its effect depends on the time-varying response. The capacitor relation is a differential equation: $$ \frac{dP}{dt} = \frac{1}{C}Q $$ Here, $P$ is the pressure across the capacitor, and $Q$ is the flow entering the capacitor. An initial capacitance can be adjusted by comparing the simulated pressure waveform with the target pressure data. For this example, a nominal value of $10^{-4} \ mL/(dyne/cm^2)$ is used for each outlet. If an overall capacitance estimate is available, allocating it in proportion to outlet area is one possible initial modeling choice, in contrast to the inverse-area resistance allocation described in the appendix. The resulting pressures and outlet flows should be checked in the three-dimensional solution. To set RCR outlet boundary conditions, modify the <Add_BC> section for each outlet cap as in this example: … <Add_BC name="cap_aorta_2"> <Type> Neumann </Type> <Time_dependence> RCR </Time_dependence> <RCR_values> <Capacitance> 1e-4 </Capacitance> <Distal_resistance> 2992.2 </Distal_resistance> <Proximal_resistance> 332.47 </Proximal_resistance> <Distal_pressure> 0 </Distal_pressure> <Initial_pressure> 0 </Initial_pressure> </RCR_values> </Add_BC> <Add_BC name="cap_right_iliac"> <Type> Neumann </Type> <Time_dependence> RCR </Time_dependence> <RCR_values> <Capacitance> 1e-4 </Capacitance> <Distal_resistance> 2425.1 </Distal_resistance> <Proximal_resistance> 269.45 </Proximal_resistance> <Distal_pressure> 0 </Distal_pressure> <Initial_pressure> 0 </Initial_pressure> </RCR_values> </Add_BC> … The XML uses the resistance values calculated in the appendix and the nominal capacitance described above. <Distal_pressure> specifies the downstream pressure reference. For a fresh run without flow-based RCR initialization, <Initial_pressure> specifies the initial capacitor pressure. Both are set to zero in this example, but they have different roles and zero is not a generally applicable choice for every model.

An initial capacitance can be adjusted by comparing the simulated pressure waveform with the target pressure data. For this example, a nominal value of \(10^{-4} \ mL/(dyne/cm^2)\) is used for each outlet. If an overall capacitance estimate is available, allocating it in proportion to outlet area is one possible initial modeling choice, in contrast to the inverse-area resistance allocation described in the appendix. The resulting pressures and outlet flows should be checked in the three-dimensional solution. To set RCR outlet boundary conditions, modify the <Add_BC> section for each outlet cap as in this example: … <Add_BC name="cap_aorta_2"> <Type> Neumann </Type> <Time_dependence> RCR </Time_dependence> <RCR_values> <Capacitance> 1e-4 </Capacitance> <Distal_resistance> 2992.2 </Distal_resistance> <Proximal_resistance> 332.47 </Proximal_resistance> <Distal_pressure> 0 </Distal_pressure> <Initial_pressure> 0 </Initial_pressure> </RCR_values> </Add_BC> <Add_BC name="cap_right_iliac"> <Type> Neumann </Type> <Time_dependence> RCR </Time_dependence> <RCR_values> <Capacitance> 1e-4 </Capacitance> <Distal_resistance> 2425.1 </Distal_resistance> <Proximal_resistance> 269.45 </Proximal_resistance> <Distal_pressure> 0 </Distal_pressure> <Initial_pressure> 0 </Initial_pressure> </RCR_values> </Add_BC> … The XML uses the resistance values calculated in the appendix and the nominal capacitance described above. <Distal_pressure> specifies the downstream pressure reference. For a fresh run without flow-based RCR initialization, <Initial_pressure> specifies the initial capacitor pressure. Both are set to zero in this example, but they have different roles and zero is not a generally applicable choice for every model.

records.title: Running svMultiPhysics in Parallel
records.text: Running svMultiPhysics in Parallel The simulation can be run as in Example 1 or in parallel using multiple processes. See Running a Simulation for the general parallel-run instructions. With MPI available, the following command runs this example using two processes: mpirun -n 2 /usr/local/sv/svMultiPhysics/2026-06-11/bin/svmultiphysics unsteady_simulation.xml The -n 2 option specifies two processes. Replace the executable path and input filename as needed for the local installation. Results are stored in 2-procs unless a different results folder is specified.

records.title: Visualizing Simulation Results
records.text: Visualizing Simulation Results Once the simulation finishes, load the saved VTK snapshots as a time series in ParaView. In this example, a snapshot is saved every ten solver time steps, not at every time step. Click “Open” in ParaView, and navigate to the results folder. The results_*.vtu files are grouped together; the down arrow expands the group to show individual files. Select the group header and click “OK” to load the complete series. Loading a series of .vtu results in ParaView. Click “Apply” on the left-hand side to load the data. By default, the results are displayed with Solid Color . As in Example 1, select a result field such as velocity or pressure from the dropdown menu at the top, and inspect its general characteristics before continuing. The 3D view displays one results file at a time. The time bar near the top of the screen selects the displayed time point: Selecting saved time points to view results in ParaView. With results saved every $10$ time steps, the one-second cycle spans $100$ output intervals. Select a saved time point by its index or use the arrow buttons on the left. Observing successive snapshots shows how the velocity and pressure fields evolve during the cardiac cycle. Line plots can also show how fields change over time. ParaView filters support operations such as clipping, slicing, integration, vector glyphs, and streamlines. The “Plot Selection Over Time” filter plots fields at a selected location across the saved time series. In the “Filters” menu, search for the filter by name or locate it in the alphabetical list. Select a location in the 3D model for the time-history plot. Left-click in the 3D view and press d to enter selection mode; the cursor should change to a “+”. For this example, select a point on an outlet cap to inspect the local velocity and pressure. A point velocity is not the integrated flow rate through the outlet, and its pressure is not necessarily the outlet's surface-averaged pressure. Those quantities require a surface calculation or corresponding boundary-output history. Selecting a point for plotting in ParaView. The selected point should highlight purple. It acts as a probe of the loaded fields at that location across the saved time points. Return to the “Plot Selection Over Time” filter on the left-hand side, and click “Apply”. ParaView may take a few moments to process the series; progress is shown at the bottom of the screen. A line graph then displays the available fields such as pressure, velocity, and wall shear stress at the selected point as functions of time: Plotting simulation fields at a point over time. The plot initially uses a single vertical axis, so fields with smaller numerical magnitudes may be difficult to see. Select which fields appear using the menu at the bottom-left of the screen. The graph data can also be exported for further analysis. Click either “Split Horizontal” or “Split Vertical” at the top-right of the graph to create another view, then select “Spreadsheet View” to show the plotted data. Select the “Plot Selection Over Time” filter in the Pipeline Browser, then choose “File > Save Data” to export a CSV file. The exported CSV data can then be plotted and analyzed using spreadsheet software or a scientific computing environment.

records.title: Unsteady Inflow Boundary Condition
records.text: Unsteady Inflow Boundary Condition The data for the unsteady inflow boundary condition is provided in a text file as a time series of volumetric flow values representing a periodic flow. The flow values are used to create the velocity vector data defining the fluid flowing into a face. The flow file has the following format: NumData NumModes T1 Q1 T2 Q2 … Tn Qn where NumData: number of time-flow pairs T1 Q1, T2 Q2, ..., Tn Qn in the file NumModes: number Fourier of modes used to represent the flow as a periodic waveform The flow for each time step is evaluated using a periodic waveform approximated using a Fourier series. Inflow data can be obtained from clinical measurements such as phase-contrast MRI. The time values in the file are in seconds. The corresponding volumetric flow rates must be in units consistent with the rest of the simulation. This example uses the centimeter-gram-second (CGS) system, with flow expressed in mL/s (equivalently, cm³/s). The figure below shows the example inlet waveform: Example unsteady inlet flow waveform. The flow into a surface face is represented using a negative value. The cap_aorta.flow inlet flow file used in this example spans one second, corresponding to 60 cycles per minute. To specify this unsteady inlet boundary condition in svMultiPhysics, modify the <Add_BC> section of the XML input file corresponding to the inlet surface. ... <Add_BC name="cap_aorta"> <Type>Dirichlet</Type> <Time_dependence>Unsteady</Time_dependence> <Temporal_values_file_path>cap_aorta.flow</Temporal_values_file_path> <Profile>Flat</Profile> <Zero_out_perimeter>true</Zero_out_perimeter> <Impose_flux>true</Impose_flux> </Add_BC> ... Compared with the steady inlet boundary condition: <Time_dependence> is changed to Unsteady . <Temporal_values_file_path> is added to reference the .flow file containing the flow data. This example also uses a Flat spatial inlet profile instead of the Parabolic profile used in Example 1. Temporal variation and spatial profile are separate settings; selecting Unsteady does not require a flat profile.

records.title: Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD)
records.text: Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) The svMultiPhysics fluid equation is used to perform computational fluid dynamics (CFD) simulations based on the incompressible Navier-Stokes equations. In this guide, CFD is used to model blood flow through the human vasculature under the rigid-wall assumption. The primary simulation outputs are pressure and velocity; secondary quantities such as wall shear stress (WSS) can also be computed and output. Boundary quantities such as outlet pressure and flow can also be written to text files and plotted to help assess whether a simulation has reached a converged solution. Creating a valid CFD simulation requires getting a lot of details right. Some familiarity with fluid mechanics is helpful for understanding how to define the physical domain, initial conditions, and boundary conditions for inlets, outlets, and walls needed to create a well-posed CFD simulation that is stable and able to accurately simulate the physical processes of interest. Some knowledge of CFD and numerical methods will also be helpful. The CFD simulations in this section model vessel walls using a rigid-wall assumption, which treats them as stationary throughout the simulation. Rigid models can approximate quantities such as pressure, but do not capture motion associated with vessel walls that deform under pulsatile pressure loads. An inflow boundary condition in a CFD simulation defines the volumetric flow rate, spatial distribution, and temporal pattern of fluid entering the computational domain. The specified flow rate is converted to a velocity field at the inlet according to the selected inflow profile, with velocity vectors normal to the inlet face. The finite element mesh is a discretization of the volume enclosed by the surface model into a set of nodes, 3D elements (tetrahedra), and element connectivity. The mesh defines the computational domain for the CFD simulation. Each mesh surface boundary is represented as a set of nodes, 2D elements (triangles), and element connectivity. The mesh files used for this section model the descending abdominal aorta with two iliac arteries obtained from imaging data. The files can be downloaded from the SimVascular DemoProject located on the SimTK website. Surface mesh of the descending abdominal aorta showing the five surfaces used to define boundary conditions.

records.title: Abdominal aortic aneurysm: geometry and mesh
records.text: Abdominal aortic aneurysm: geometry and mesh In this guide, we solve the clinical case of an abdominal aortic aneurysm. The geometrical models of the solid and the fluid are shown in the figure below. Solid (left) and fluid (right) models of the abdominal aortic aneurysm case. The fluid domain was obtained from segmenting a medical image, and the solid domain was obtained by extruding the lumen wall of the fluid domain by a constant thickness. For more details on how to generate a patient-specific model look into the modeling section. The surface mesh for fluid domain, for the solid domain and the inlet section of the combined meshes are shown in the figure below. Solid (left) and fluid (centre) meshes are first created separately, and then used in svMultiPhysics to perform Fluid-Structure-Interaction simulations with Arbitrary Lagrangian–Eulerian (ALE) coordinates. The right figure represent the inlet section of the combined meshes showing the boundary layer refinement for the fluid mesh and the solid mesh. It is not the purpose of this guide to illustrate the process of mesh creation for FSI problems, but it is important to state that the interface between the solid mesh (inner wall) and fluid mesh (lumen wall) match. Meaning the lumen_wall of the fluid mesh and the inner_wall of the solid mesh should be exactly the same.
